name: Red Hat, Inc.
origin_detail: Bob Young's ACC Corporation (Connecticut, 1993; Red Hat gives 26 Mar 1993 as its founding date) merged with Marc Ewing's Red Hat Linux distribution (North Carolina, 1994) to form Red Hat Software in 1995; HQ Raleigh, NC
openness_notes: Products are GPL/OSI-licensed and sold as subscriptions (support, certification, updates). Licences never changed, but access narrowed: Dec 2020 CentOS Linux (free 1:1 RHEL rebuild) was ended in favour of CentOS Stream; Jun 2023 CentOS Stream became the sole public source for RHEL-related code and RHEL sources went to the customer portal only. Still level 3, but the trend is toward limiting free downstream rebuilds.

license_history.note: Ewing's distribution, sold on CD with support

license_history.license: CentOS (GPL rebuild of RHEL) joins Red Hat

license_history.license: GPL unchanged; RHEL source distribution restricted
license_history.note: CentOS Stream made sole public repository for RHEL-related source; customers get sources via Customer Portal

relicensing_events.fork_backer: Rocky Linux founded by CentOS co-founder Gregory Kurtzer (CIQ); AlmaLinux by CloudLinux
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Not a licence change. Announced 8 Dec 2020 that CentOS Linux 8 would end at end of 2021; community response overwhelmingly negative; rebuild forks launched within weeks

relicensing_events.to: CentOS Stream as sole public source; RHEL sources only to subscribers
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Not a licence change (GPL). Rocky Linux turned to UBI images and cloud instances for sources; AlmaLinux dropped 1:1 bug-for-bug goal for ABI compatibility; OpenELA formed as a 501(c)(6) to publish sources

exit_events.note: IPO 11 Aug 1999; at the time the eighth-biggest first-day gain in Wall Street history
Closed 9 Jul 2019 at $190/share cash (~63% premium); announced Oct 2018; IBM's largest deal; Red Hat kept as a distinct unit in Raleigh

risk_events: Dec 2020: CentOS Linux discontinued in favour of CentOS Stream; user backlash; Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux forks
Jun 2023: RHEL public sources restricted to CentOS Stream; Oracle, SUSE and CIQ formed OpenELA (Aug 2023)
Sep 2025: Red Hat legal, HR, finance and accounting functions to move into IBM from 2026 (engineering kept separate for now)
Q4 2025: Red Hat (IBM Hybrid Cloud) growth slowed to 10% from 16% (Q2) and 14% (Q3); US federal shutdown cited
Apr 2026: reports (weakly sourced) of Red Hat closing its China engineering team and moving work to India
robustness: Highly robust commercially: survived the dot-com bust as a public company, then became IBM's core software growth engine (exit run-rate ~$7.5B ARR at end-2025 per IBM's Q4 2025 call; OpenShift ARR ~$1.9B, >30% growth). Code is GPL and upstream-first (Fedora, CentOS Stream, kernel), so the software would outlive the firm; but the RHEL brand, certification ecosystem and build pipeline are single-vendor, now increasingly absorbed into IBM.
physical_science_relevance: RHEL and its rebuilds (formerly CentOS, now Rocky/AlmaLinux) are the default OS of many HPC clusters and national-lab systems; the CentOS changes forced scientific computing sites to migrate.
openness_effect_assessment: Openness was the product: a fully GPL distribution monetized through subscriptions scaled to ~$3.4B revenue (FY2019) and a $34B exit, the largest open-source acquisition. The same openness let free 1:1 rebuilds (CentOS, then Rocky/Alma) capture users who would not pay; Red Hat's 2020 and 2023 restrictions reduced that leakage without changing licences, at the cost of community trust, competitor coalitions (OpenELA) and forks, with no visible revenue damage (Red Hat growth stayed at 10-16% in 2025).
key_takeaway: Red Hat is the canonical proof that a pure open-source (level 3) business can reach large scale, longevity (30+ years) and a top-tier exit. Its later history shows the main risk of that model is not competitors closing the code but downstream clones freely reusing it; Red Hat's answer was to restrict distribution channels rather than relicense, keeping OSI licences while tightening control, and post-acquisition integration into IBM is now the main threat to its independent culture.
